---
title: "Session initialization"
sidebar: start
---

Every BF session **must** start by importing `bf` and initializing the BF object. This single object is the gateway to everything: data handling, model definition, fitting, diagnostics, and saving.

> **Rule:** Always import `bf` **before** importing `jax` or any other JAX-dependent module, so that the XLA configuration is applied first.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python
```python
from BayesForge import bf

m = bf(
    platform="cpu",          # "cpu", "gpu", or "tpu"
    cores=None,              # CPU cores (None = all available)
    float_precision=64,      # 64 for float64, 32 for float32
    rand_seed=42,            # int for reproducibility, True for random
    gpu_index=None,          # GPU index when platform="gpu"
    deallocate=False,        # deallocate existing device first
    print_devices_found=True,# print device info on init
)
```

## R
```r
library(BayesForge)

m <- importBF(
    platform = "cpu",            # "cpu", "gpu", or "tpu"
    cores = NULL,                # CPU cores (NULL = all available)
    rand_seed = 42,              # integer for reproducibility, TRUE for random
    deallocate = FALSE,          # deallocate existing device first
    print_devices_found = TRUE   # print device info on init
)
```

## Julia
```julia
using PyBayesForge

m = importBF(
    platform = "cpu",            # "cpu", "gpu", or "tpu"
    cores = nothing,             # CPU cores (nothing = all available)
    rand_seed = 42,              # integer for reproducibility, true for random
    deallocate = false,          # deallocate existing device first
    print_devices_found = true,  # print device info on init
)
```
:::

### Arguments

| Argument | Type | Default | Description |
|----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `platform` | str | `"cpu"` | Hardware backend: `"cpu"`, `"gpu"`, or `"tpu"` |
| `cores` | int | `None` | CPU cores to allocate (`None` = all). Only for `platform="cpu"` |
| `float_precision` | int or str | `64` | JAX floating-point precision. Pass `64` (`"float64"`) or `32` (`"float32"`) |
| `rand_seed` | int or bool | `True` | Reproducibility seed. Pass an `int` (e.g. `42`) for reproducible results, or `True` for entropy-based randomness |
| `gpu_index` | int | `None` | Which GPU to use by index. Only for `platform="gpu"` |
| `deallocate` | bool | `False` | Deallocate existing device before setting up new configuration |
| `print_devices_found` | bool | `True` | Print detected devices on initialization |
| `backend` | str | `"numpyro"` | Inference backend: `"numpyro"` or `"tfp"` |

In R and Julia, `importBF()` takes the same arguments except `float_precision` and `gpu_index` (Python only); `NULL` (R) and `nothing` (Julia) stand for Python's `None`.

### Common initialization patterns

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python
```python
# Reproducible CPU session (default for development)
m = bf(platform="cpu", rand_seed=42, float_precision=64)

# Multi-core CPU for parallel chains
m = bf(platform="cpu", cores=8, rand_seed=42)

# 32-bit precision for memory efficiency
m = bf(platform="cpu", rand_seed=42, float_precision=32)
```

```{.python .no-test}
# GPU with specific device (Linux/WSL2 with an NVIDIA GPU)
m = bf(platform="gpu", gpu_index=0, rand_seed=42)
```

## R
```r
# Reproducible CPU session (default for development)
m <- importBF(platform = "cpu", rand_seed = 42)

# Multi-core CPU for parallel chains
m <- importBF(platform = "cpu", cores = 8, rand_seed = 42)
```

```{.r .no-test}
# GPU (Linux/WSL2 with an NVIDIA GPU; environment created with setup_env(backend = "gpu"))
m <- importBF(platform = "gpu", rand_seed = 42)
```

## Julia
```julia
# Reproducible CPU session (default for development)
m = importBF(platform = "cpu", rand_seed = 42)

# Multi-core CPU for parallel chains
m = importBF(platform = "cpu", cores = 8, rand_seed = 42)
```

```{.julia .no-test}
# GPU (Linux/WSL2 with an NVIDIA GPU; GPU build of JAX added with CondaPkg)
m = importBF(platform = "gpu", rand_seed = 42)
```
:::

---

## Saving and reusing a BF object

After fitting a model, save the complete BF object to disk. This persists the model, data, posteriors, and full sampler state — allowing you to reload and analyze later without re-fitting.

### Save

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python
```{.python .no-test}
m.save("/path/to/my_model.pkl")
# Default filename: "{model_name}_bf.pkl" in current directory
```

## R
```{.r .no-test}
# A model written in R cannot be pickled: m$save() raises
# "TypeError: cannot pickle 'PyCapsule' object". Save the draws instead:
saveRDS(bf_draws(m), "/path/to/my_model_draws.rds")
```

## Julia
```{.julia .no-test}
m.save("/path/to/my_model.pkl")
# Default filename: "{model_name}_bf.pkl" in current directory
```
:::

### Load

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python
```{.python .no-test}
m = bf.load("/path/to/my_model.pkl")
```

## R
```{.r .no-test}
draws <- readRDS("/path/to/my_model_draws.rds")   # draws saved from R
# A bf object saved from Python or Julia loads with:
m <- reticulate::import("BayesForge")$bf$load("/path/to/my_model.pkl")
```

## Julia
```{.julia .no-test}
using PythonCall
m = PyBayesForge.BFObject(pyimport("BayesForge").bf.load("/path/to/my_model.pkl"))
```
:::

Once loaded, you can access:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python
```{.python .no-test}
m.posteriors        # Posterior samples
m.posteriors_full   # Full posterior (before any filtering)
m.summary()         # Posterior summary table
m.data_on_model     # Data used in the fit
m.model             # Model function
m.diag              # Diagnostic tools
```

## R
```{.r .no-test}
m$posteriors        # Posterior samples
m$posteriors_full   # Full posterior (before any filtering)
m$summary()         # Posterior summary table
m$data_on_model     # Data used in the fit
m$model             # Model function
m$diag              # Diagnostic tools
```

## Julia
```{.julia .no-test}
m.posteriors        # Posterior samples
m.posteriors_full   # Full posterior (before any filtering)
m.summary()         # Posterior summary table
m.data_on_model     # Data used in the fit
m.model             # Model function
m.diag              # Diagnostic tools
```
:::

### Workflow with save/load

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python
```python
# --- Session 1: Fit and save ---
import jax.numpy as jnp
from BayesForge import bf
m = bf(platform="cpu", rand_seed=42)

x = jnp.linspace(-1, 1, 40)
y = 0.5 + 2.0 * x + 0.1 * jnp.cos(7 * x)

def model(x, y):
    alpha = m.dist.normal(0, 10, name="alpha")
    beta  = m.dist.normal(0, 1, name="beta")
    sigma = m.dist.exponential(1, name="sigma")
    m.dist.normal(alpha + beta * x, sigma, obs=y)

m.fit(model, obs=dict(x=x, y=y))
m.save("linear_regression.pkl")

# --- Session 2: Load and analyze (no re-fit) ---
from BayesForge import bf
m = bf.load("linear_regression.pkl")
print(m.summary())
print(m.posteriors["beta"].mean())
```

## R
```r
# --- Session 1: Fit and save the draws ---
library(BayesForge)
m <- importBF(platform = "cpu", rand_seed = 42)

x <- seq(-1, 1, length.out = 40)
y <- 0.5 + 2.0 * x + 0.1 * cos(7 * x)

model <- function(x, y) {
    alpha <- bf.dist.normal(0, 10, name = "alpha")
    beta  <- bf.dist.normal(0, 1, name = "beta")
    sigma <- bf.dist.exponential(1, name = "sigma")
    bf.dist.normal(alpha + beta * x, sigma, obs = y)
}

m$fit(model, obs = list(x = jnp$array(x), y = jnp$array(y)))
saveRDS(bf_draws(m), "linear_regression_draws.rds")

# --- Session 2: Load and analyze (no re-fit) ---
draws <- readRDS("linear_regression_draws.rds")
print(posterior::summarise_draws(posterior::as_draws_df(draws)))
print(mean(draws$beta))
```

## Julia
```julia
# --- Session 1: Fit and save ---
using PyBayesForge, PythonCall
m = importBF(platform = "cpu", rand_seed = 42)

x = collect(range(-1, 1; length = 40))
y = 0.5 .+ 2.0 .* x .+ 0.1 .* cos.(7 .* x)

@BF function model(x, y)
    alpha = m.dist.normal(0, 10, name = "alpha")
    beta  = m.dist.normal(0, 1, name = "beta")
    sigma = m.dist.exponential(1, name = "sigma")
    m.dist.normal(alpha + beta * x, sigma, obs = y)
end

m.fit(model, obs = pydict(x = jnp.array(x), y = jnp.array(y)))
m.save("linear_regression.pkl")

# --- Session 2: Load and analyze (no re-fit) ---
using PyBayesForge, PythonCall
m = PyBayesForge.BFObject(pyimport("BayesForge").bf.load("linear_regression.pkl"))
println(m.summary())
println(m.posteriors["beta"].mean())
```
:::

> **Note:** The object is serialized with `cloudpickle` (from Python and Julia; a model written in R cannot be serialized, so save its draws with `saveRDS(bf_draws(m), ...)`), so the full model closure and sampler state are preserved. The saved `.pkl` file is self-contained and portable.
